GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats

Shahaf Valencia Levy shahaf.valenciale@mail.huji.ac.il Affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem    Sagie Benaim sagie.benaim@mail.huji.ac.il Affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
Abstract

Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: https://svlwoof.github.io/gaussianrenderformer.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) has become a common way to represent real scenes captured from photos. A 3DGS scene is a set of Gaussians, each with a position, scale, rotation, color and opacity, and every image of it is produced by a rasterizer: a hand-written algorithm that projects the Gaussians onto the image plane and blends them. In this paper we replace that algorithm with a neural network.11 1 Large language models assisted both the research behind this paper, including code and the analysis of experiments, and its writing. The authors take full responsibility for its content. Given a set of Gaussians and a camera, our model outputs the image directly, without per-scene optimization and with no rasterizer in the renderer (Figure 1).

Learned rendering has made significant progress for other kinds of scene descriptions. RenderFormer (Zeng et al., 2025) renders triangle meshes with global illumination using a transformer, and RenderFormer-V2 (Zeng et al., 2026) extends it to more kinds of primitives, lights and media. For Gaussians, to our knowledge, no learned renderer exists. Methods that reconstruct, refine, relight or analyze Gaussians still hand the final image to a hand-written renderer, usually the 3DGS rasterizer itself (Section 2).

A learned renderer of Gaussians could offer what a rasterizer does not. It could learn light transport from data, as RenderFormer does for meshes, where relightable Gaussian methods rely on a hand-written shading model and approximate the indirect light (Gao et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a). It could render captured splats together with meshes and lights in one model, as RenderFormer-V2 does for meshes, media and lights. It has no sorting step, so it avoids the popping that sorting causes as the camera moves. And it could learn a prior that fills in what its input lacks. None of this is shown here: a network first has to render Gaussians at all.

It is also not obvious that the approach that works for meshes carries over to Gaussians. Gaussians have no surface or material, are semi-transparent and overlap heavily. An object typically needs tens of thousands, while RenderFormer was trained on scenes of up to 4,096 triangles. A learned renderer has to resolve which Gaussians are visible and how they blend at every pixel, which a rasterizer does by sorting them.

We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that renders Gaussians directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token, and a view-independent encoder lets these tokens exchange information. A view-dependent decoder then represents each small patch of the image by a token built from the camera rays passing through it. These tokens attend to the Gaussians and are told where in the image each Gaussian lands and how large it appears there, both computed per Gaussian, while everything per pixel is learned. We start from RenderFormer’s pretrained weights and train on 26,820 objects from Objaverse (Deitke et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025), each pruned to 20,000 Gaussians.

We treat this as a feasibility study at the object level. On 300 objects never seen in training, GaussianRenderFormer reaches 38.08 dB PSNR against renders of the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB (Section 6). For context, LVSM (Jin et al., 2025), the closest rasterizer-free transformer, reaches 32.36 dB with its decoder-only variant on Google Scanned Objects at 512 pixels from four input images, and GS-LRM (Zhang et al., 2024), which rasterizes, 30.52 dB, both as reported in LVSM’s Table 1. They start from images and we from the splat, so the numbers are not directly comparable, but they show the range in which learned renderers of objects work. The gap to rasterization is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder, though under-training is not ruled out.

Our contributions are (1) GaussianRenderFormer, to our knowledge the first feed-forward neural renderer for 3D Gaussian splats with no rasterizer in the renderer, (2) three changes that adapt a mesh renderer’s view decoder to Gaussians, a 2D rotary embedding of where each Gaussian lands in the image, its projected footprint on the attention keys and smaller patches, each ablated at moderate scale and again at full scale, together with a schedule that trains the new input layer first, and (3) an analysis of the remaining gap to rasterization, which is not a generalization gap and is consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder, and of how the model behaves outside its training setup. The code and the trained models are available at https://github.com/SVLwoof/gaussianformer.

2 Related Work

Rendering 3D Gaussians. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a scene by projecting each Gaussian onto the image plane and alpha-blending the sorted projections, a process evolved from EWA splatting (Zwicker et al., 2002). Later works improve this rasterizer against aliasing (Yu et al., 2024), with flat disks (Huang et al., 2024) or with per-pixel sorting (Radl et al., 2024), and gsplat (Ye et al., 2025)22 2 https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat is the optimized open-source implementation we use to render our ground truth. Other works ray-trace Gaussians (Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024) or replace them with ellipsoids that can be ray-traced exactly (Mai et al., 2025), and Sort-free Gaussian Splatting (Hou et al., 2025) learns weights that replace the sorting but keeps the projection and blending of a rasterizer. All of these are hand-written algorithms, while GaussianRenderFormer renders with a network.

Learned renderers for explicit scenes. The works closest to ours render an explicit description of a scene with a network instead of an algorithm. RenderFormer renders triangle meshes with global illumination (Section 3.2), and RenderFormer-V2 (Zeng et al., 2026) and RenderFormer++ (Du et al., 2026) extend it to more primitives, lights and media and to object-level tokens, but none of them takes Gaussians. Pointersect (Chang et al., 2023) renders point clouds with a transformer per ray, Xu et al. (2026) predict indirect illumination from sampled points, and RenderNet (Nguyen-Phuoc et al., 2018) rendered voxel grids and the Generative Query Network (Eslami et al., 2018) a learned scene code. Most other neural rendering methods keep a conventional renderer and are optimized per scene: deferred neural rendering (Thies et al., 2019) and neural point-based graphics (Aliev et al., 2020; Rückert et al., 2022; Franke et al., 2024) rasterize learned features before a network produces the image, and Point-NeRF (Xu et al., 2022) ray-marches neural points. To our knowledge, GaussianRenderFormer is the first model to render a given set of 3D Gaussians with a network alone.

Networks around Gaussian splatting. Most learned models that involve 3D Gaussians produce them rather than render them. Feed-forward reconstruction methods predict Gaussians from a set of images in a single pass and then rasterize them (Szymanowicz et al., 2024; Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Jiang et al., 2025b). Other models take Gaussians as input tokens for other tasks, such as self-supervised pretraining (Ma et al., 2025), scene understanding (Li et al., 2025), generative modeling (Gao et al., 2025) or refining the Gaussians themselves (Chen et al., 2025b), and relightable methods shade them with a hand-written model (Gao et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024), which GI-GS (Chen et al., 2025a) extends with an approximation of the indirect light. Wherever these methods produce an image, a rasterizer still renders it, while for GaussianRenderFormer the Gaussians are the input and the image is the output.

View synthesis without explicit geometry. Another line of work synthesizes new views without any explicit 3D representation, mostly with transformers. The Scene Representation Transformer (Sajjadi et al., 2022) decodes each pixel from a ray that attends to latent tokens of posed images, Light Field Networks (Sitzmann et al., 2021), Light Field Neural Rendering (Suhail et al., 2022) and GNT (Varma T et al., 2023) map rays to colors directly or with attention along each ray, and LVSM (Jin et al., 2025) and RayZer (Jiang et al., 2025a) scale this idea to large models. These are the closest relatives of GaussianRenderFormer: most of them decode scene tokens with ray queries, and none uses a rasterizer. Their scene, however, is given only through images, while ours is explicit Gaussians, so our output can be compared directly with rasterizing the same input.

3 Background

3.1 3D Gaussian Splatting

3DGS represents a scene as a set of NN Gaussians, fitted to photos by gradient descent. Gaussian ii has a center 𝝁i∈ℝ3\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, a covariance 𝚺i=𝐑i​𝐒i​𝐒i⊤​𝐑i⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{i}^{\top} built from a rotation 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i} (a unit quaternion 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i}) and per-axis scales 𝐒i=diag⁡(𝐬i)\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}_{i}), an opacity oi∈[0,1]o_{i}\in[0,1] and a color 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i}. To render an image, the rasterizer projects each Gaussian to a 2D Gaussian with center 𝝁i′\bm{\mu}^{\prime}_{i} and covariance 𝚺i′=𝐉𝐖​𝚺i​𝐖⊤​𝐉⊤\bm{\Sigma}^{\prime}_{i}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\bm{\Sigma}_{i}\mathbf{W}^{\top}\mathbf{J}^{\top}, where 𝐖\mathbf{W} is the camera’s rotation and 𝐉\mathbf{J} the Jacobian of the projection, sorts the Gaussians by depth and blends them front to back at every pixel 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

𝐂⁡(𝐱)=∑i=1N𝐜i​αi​(𝐱)​∏j=1i−1(1−αj​(𝐱)),αi​(𝐱)=oi​exp⁡(−12​(𝐱−𝝁i′)⊤​𝚺i′−1​(𝐱−𝝁i′)).\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{c}_{i}\,\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{x})\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}\bigl(1-\alpha_{j}(\mathbf{x})\bigr),\qquad\alpha_{i}(\mathbf{x})=o_{i}\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu}^{\prime}_{i})^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{\prime-1}_{i}(\mathbf{x}-\bm{\mu}^{\prime}_{i})\Bigr). (1)

This is the computation GaussianRenderFormer replaces. Of the color, which 3DGS stores as spherical harmonics that change with the viewing direction, we use only the view-independent part, a single RGB value, in the input and the ground truth.

3.2 RenderFormer

RenderFormer renders a triangle mesh with a transformer in two stages. In the view-independent stage, each triangle becomes one token, built by a linear layer from its vertex normals and its material, and 12 layers of self-attention over these tokens and 16 register tokens model how light travels between triangles. Positions enter only through a rotary position embedding (Su et al., 2024) of the triangles’ vertices in the attention. In the view-dependent stage, each patch of 8×88\times 8 pixels becomes one token, built by a linear layer from the directions of its 64 rays. Six layers of cross-attention to the triangle tokens, with the triangles’ positions in the camera’s frame, each followed by self-attention among the ray-bundle tokens, gather what every patch sees, and a DPT head (Ranftl et al., 2021) turns them into pixels of high dynamic range radiance, encoded as log10⁡(1+x)\log_{10}(1+x). RenderFormer is trained on scenes of up to 4,096 triangles, first at 256 and then at 512 pixels. GaussianRenderFormer keeps this layout and its pretrained weights (Section 4).

4 Method

GaussianRenderFormer keeps RenderFormer’s two-stage layout (Section 3.2) and starts from its pretrained weights. We change the first stage so that each token is a Gaussian instead of a triangle, and how the second stage looks at the scene, so that it can handle tens of thousands of semi-transparent Gaussians: it is told where each Gaussian lands in the image and how large it appears there. Figure 2 shows the full model.

4.1 Gaussian tokens and the scene encoder

Each Gaussian is described by a vector of 14 numbers,

𝐠i=[𝝁i,𝐬i,𝐪i,𝐜i,oi]∈ℝ14,\mathbf{g}_{i}=\bigl[\,\bm{\mu}_{i},\;\mathbf{s}_{i},\;\mathbf{q}_{i},\;\mathbf{c}_{i},\;o_{i}\,\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{14}, (2)

holding its center (3), scales (3), rotation quaternion (4), color (3) and opacity (1). The token of Gaussian ii is

𝐭i=𝐞+RMSNorm⁡(𝐀𝐠i+𝐛),\mathbf{t}_{i}=\mathbf{e}+\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{g}_{i}+\mathbf{b}), (3)

where 𝐀∈ℝ768×14\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{768\times 14} and 𝐛\mathbf{b} are a linear layer followed by RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), and 𝐞\mathbf{e} is a learned embedding shared by all Gaussian tokens. The token embeds all 14 numbers, the center included, so it changes with the random rotation of every training sample (Section 4.3). This input layer replaces RenderFormer’s triangle embedding, and it is the only new part of the model apart from the footprint layers (Section 4.2), which start at zero. In addition, the encoder’s self-attention applies a 3D rotary position embedding of each Gaussian’s center, where RenderFormer used the triangle’s vertices. The 16 register tokens sit at the mean center of the Gaussians. The rest of the scene encoder, 12 self-attention layers, is unchanged and runs once per object, whatever the number of views.

4.2 The view decoder

The view decoder follows RenderFormer: each image patch is a token built from the directions of the rays through its pixels, and six layers of cross-attention to the scene tokens and self-attention among the patches turn these tokens into pixels through a DPT head. Inside it, the Gaussians’ centers are expressed in the camera’s frame and enter the attention through the same 3D rotary embedding. We make three changes.

2D rotary embedding of projected positions. A 3D position embedding tells the decoder where a Gaussian is relative to the camera, but not where it lands in the image, which is what a patch needs to know. We therefore project each Gaussian’s center into the view,

ui=1p​(W2+f​xizi),vi=1p​(H2−f​yizi),u_{i}=\frac{1}{p}\Bigl(\frac{W}{2}+f\frac{x_{i}}{z_{i}}\Bigr),\qquad v_{i}=\frac{1}{p}\Bigl(\frac{H}{2}-f\frac{y_{i}}{z_{i}}\Bigr), (4)

where (xi,yi,zi)(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i}) is the center in camera coordinates, ff the focal length in pixels, W×HW\times H the image size and pp the patch size, so (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}) is measured in patches. In the cross-attention, the keys of each Gaussian are rotated by a 2D rotary embedding of (ui,vi)(u_{i},v_{i}) and the query of each patch by the same embedding of the patch’s center, so the attention between a patch and a Gaussian depends on the distance between them in the image. The patches’ self-attention uses the same 2D embedding. It rotates 8 channel pairs per image axis in each attention head, pairs that the 3D embedding leaves unrotated, at 8 frequencies from 0.25 to 1.75 radians per patch, so the pretrained 3D embedding is kept as it is.

Smaller patches. RenderFormer uses patches of 8×88\times 8 pixels. We use 4×44\times 4 pixels, which gives the decoder four times as many tokens per image and lets it resolve finer detail. To reuse the pretrained ray embedding, which expects the 64 ray directions of an 8×88\times 8 patch, we upsample each 4×44\times 4 patch’s ray directions to 8×88\times 8 by nearest-neighbor interpolation before embedding them. This is the same as an embedding of the 48 numbers of a 4×44\times 4 patch whose weights are the pretrained ones summed over each 2×22\times 2 block. The DPT head upsamples its output to the image size whatever the patch size.

Projected footprint on the keys. The rotary embeddings tell the decoder where each Gaussian’s center lands, but not how far the Gaussian reaches in the image. Its scale and rotation reach the decoder only through the scene tokens, which are the same for every view, so the decoder would have to work out each Gaussian’s apparent size and shape for every camera. We give it directly. With 𝚺i=𝐑i​diag⁡(𝐬i)2​𝐑i⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}_{i})^{2}\mathbf{R}_{i}^{\top} the Gaussian’s covariance in camera coordinates and 𝐉i\mathbf{J}_{i} the Jacobian of the projection of Eq. 4 at its center, its footprint in the image, in patches, is the 2×22\times 2 covariance

𝚺i′=𝐉i​𝚺i​𝐉i⊤+0.3p2​𝐈,𝐉i=fp​zi​(10−xi/zi0−1yi/zi),\bm{\Sigma}^{\prime}_{i}=\mathbf{J}_{i}\bm{\Sigma}_{i}\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\top}+\frac{0.3}{p^{2}}\mathbf{I},\qquad\mathbf{J}_{i}=\frac{f}{p\,z_{i}}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-x_{i}/z_{i}\\ 0&-1&y_{i}/z_{i}\end{pmatrix}, (5)

the same projection that 3DGS applies before rasterizing (Kerbl et al., 2023), where the small isotropic term (0.3 square pixels) is the low-pass filter of the gsplat rasterizer (Ye et al., 2025). Without it the model is only 0.08 dB worse (Section 6.2). We describe it by four numbers, the logarithms of its two standard deviations and (cos⁡2​θ,sin⁡2​θ)(\cos 2\theta,\sin 2\theta) for the angle θ\theta of its major axis, each clipped to [−6,6][-6,6]. In each decoder layer, a linear layer maps these four numbers to a vector that is added to the Gaussian’s key in the cross-attention, so the footprint changes which Gaussians a patch attends to but not what it reads from them. Adding it to the values as well helps on our ablation harness, but we keep it in the keys only for the reasons given in Section 6.2. Register tokens and Gaussians behind the camera get zeros. These linear layers are new and initialized to zero, so the model starts from exactly the function it had without them.

The projected center and footprint are computed in closed form for each Gaussian from its parameters and the camera, a change of coordinates like expressing each triangle’s vertices in the camera’s frame for RenderFormer’s decoder. Nothing is computed per pixel: which Gaussians cover a pixel, which of them are visible, how they blend and what color results are left to the network.

The first two changes add no parameters and the third only 23,040, initialized to zero, but the first two change what the pretrained layers compute, which the short stage 3 at 256×256256\times 256 pixels recovers (Section 4.3).

4.3 Training

The model is trained to reproduce renders of the full, unpruned splat from a version pruned to 20,000 Gaussians (Section 5). The model outputs colors in the log encoding log10⁡(1+𝐈)\log_{10}(1+\mathbf{I}) inherited from RenderFormer, and the loss combines an L1 term in that encoding with LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) on a VGG backbone:

ℒ=(1−λ)​ℒ1w​(𝐈^,log10⁡(1+𝐈))+λ​ℒLPIPS​(10𝐈^−1,𝐈),λ=0.5,\mathcal{L}=(1-\lambda)\,\mathcal{L}_{1}^{w}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{I}},\log_{10}(1+\mathbf{I})\bigr)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\bigl(10^{\hat{\mathbf{I}}}-1,\mathbf{I}\bigr),\qquad\lambda=0.5, (6)

where 𝐈^\hat{\mathbf{I}} is the model’s output and 𝐈\mathbf{I} the target image. ℒ1w\mathcal{L}_{1}^{w} is the L1 distance averaged over pixels with a weight of 1 on the object and 0.050.05 on the background, since an object covers only a few percent of the image. Every training sample rotates the object and its camera by the same random rotation, which leaves the image unchanged but keeps the model from relying on a fixed orientation.

Training runs in four stages (Table 1). The final model’s first two stages differ slightly from this recipe (Appendix G). The first trains only the new input layer, with the rest of RenderFormer frozen. The second trains the whole model at 256×256256\times 256 pixels. The third switches on the three changes above for a short recovery at the same resolution, and the fourth trains at 512×512512\times 512 pixels with LPIPS. We use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with a weight decay of 0.01, a batch of 8 views on 8 GPUs, and a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} (10−310^{-3} in the first stage), held constant after a short warmup and decayed with a cosine over the last steps of each stage.

5 Data

Source. We train on Objaverse_Splats33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/ShapeSplats/Objaverse_Splats, the subset of ShapeSplat with a trained 3DGS splat per Objaverse object. We use only splats that fit their object well according to ShapeSplat’s metadata, with a PSNR of at least 32 dB and an LPIPS of at most 0.06, and that have exactly 50,000 Gaussians. From these we draw 30,000 objects for training and 2,000 for validation, and drop objects that are degenerate or nearly transparent (maximum opacity below 0.4). This leaves 26,820 training objects and 1,806 validation objects.

Normalization. Each splat is centered on the median position of its Gaussians, rotated so that its up axis is +y+y, and scaled uniformly so that its largest coordinate is 0.45, which places every object in [−0.45,0.45]3[-0.45,0.45]^{3}. We keep only the view-independent color of each Gaussian (Section 3.1).

Ground truth. For every object we render 28 views of the full, unpruned splat with gsplat at 512×512512\times 512 pixels, with a 45∘45^{\circ} field of view and a black background. The cameras orbit the object and look at its center: 14 at a distance of 1.7, and 7 each at 1.15 and 2.45. Consecutive cameras alternate between looking down at the object and slightly up at it, to see its top and its bottom. Every object has the same 28 cameras.

Input preparation. The full splats have 50,000 Gaussians, while the model takes 20,000. We keep the 20,000 Gaussians with the highest importance score adapted from LightGaussian (Fan et al., 2024), which sums each Gaussian’s opacity times its projected area over 64 orbit views and slightly favors larger Gaussians. Pruning alone leaves holes and darkens the object, so we then fine-tune the kept Gaussians for 1,500 steps to match renders of the full splat from those 64 views, with the usual 3DGS loss (L1 plus 0.2 times D-SSIM (Wang et al., 2004)) and without adding or removing any Gaussians. This takes about 10 seconds per object on one GPU. The 64 views lie at the same distance as the main evaluation views, but at different angles. The model never sees the full splat, only the pruned one, and is trained to reproduce the renders of the full splat. A rasterizer can render the pruned input directly. We call this gsplat on the input, and use it as the bar for the model throughout Section 6, while the reference is always the render of the full splat.

Splits. Of the 1,806 validation objects, 100 monitor the validation loss during training, and 300 others, never seen in training, are the held-out objects on which we evaluated every design decision. We call them the development held-out set. For the main result, we draw 300 further objects at random from the remaining 1,406, never used during development: the fresh held-out set. We also evaluate 300 training objects.

6 Experiments

Setup. All images are 512×512512\times 512 pixels with a 45∘45^{\circ} field of view. Both the model’s input and the ground truth use only the view-independent color of each Gaussian. We report PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), with LPIPS computed on an AlexNet backbone (the training loss uses VGG). The main result is on the fresh held-out objects, over all 28 views of the training setup. Unless stated otherwise, every other number is the mean over the 300 development held-out objects, 4 views each at distance 1.7. Since the object covers only a small part of the image, every metric is computed on the evaluation crop: the square around the object in the reference (pixels brighter than 0.02), with a 12-pixel margin, resized to 512×512512\times 512. The black background inside the crop is easy for both renderers, so we also report masked PSNR, over the pixels where the full splat’s opacity exceeds 0.5, on the whole image. We compare against two references. The first is a rasterization of the full, unpruned splat, which is the image the model is trained to produce. The second is a rasterization of the pruned 20,000-Gaussian input, which is exactly what the input encodes.

6.1 Main result

Table 2 shows the main result, on 300 held-out objects that we never used during development. Over all 28 views at the three training distances, GaussianRenderFormer reaches 38.08 dB against the unpruned render, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap depends on the camera distance, from 3.9 dB at 1.15 to 6.8 dB at 1.7. Rasterizing the input is best at 1.7, the distance of the 64 views the pruned input was fine-tuned on (Section 5), while the model is nearly flat across distances. Masked PSNR, which leaves out the black background, is about 5 dB lower for both, with about the same gap. Figure 3 shows three held-out objects, at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of the model’s score. The model’s errors concentrate on edges and fine texture, while its colors and shapes are right.

The gap is not one of generalization. On the development held-out objects, on which we chose our design, the model scores the same, 38.02 dB, so choosing on them did not inflate the result. On 300 training objects, over their 28 training views, it scores only 0.17 dB higher than on unseen objects. These are the exact images the model was trained to produce, from the exact same input, and it still stays 5.9 dB below rasterizing that input. Nor does the gap come from what pruning removed: measured against a rasterization of its own input instead of the unpruned render, the model scores only 0.3 dB higher (4 views at distance 1.7). Its error is in rendering the input it has. Each training image was seen only about four times in the final stage, though, so an under-trained model would show the same. Sections 6.3 and 6.4 ask where the gap comes from.

Cost. GaussianRenderFormer is much slower than a rasterizer (Table 3). On one L40S GPU, a single view takes 275 ms, more than half of it in the scene encoder. The encoder runs once per object, so every further view in the same call adds about 135 ms. gsplat renders the same input in under a millisecond.

The gap in cost grows with the number of Gaussians (Appendix C.3). The scene encoder attends from every Gaussian to every other, so the model’s time grows roughly with the square of the input size: one view of 640,000 Gaussians takes 75 s instead of 275 ms at 20,000. Its memory grows roughly linearly, to 23.7 GB at 640,000 Gaussians, while gsplat stays under 3 ms and 0.1 GB of working memory.

6.2 Ablations

Training the final model took 1,327 GPU-hours, so we do not repeat it for every change. Our earlier probes trained on 10 objects, and their results did not carry over to larger training sets. We therefore test every change on one harness of moderate scale. It trains on 1,000 objects from the end of stage 2 (Table 1), with short versions of stages 3 and 4 (Appendix C.1). Every arm is evaluated on the 300 held-out objects and on its own training objects, and differs from the harness with all changes, the recipe of the final model, in one change only (Table 4). The end of stage 2 has 8×88\times 8 patches, no 2D embedding and no footprint, so the arm with all changes has to learn all three in these steps, while the ablated arms have less to learn. This favors the ablated arms. Every arm is a single run. To see how far two runs of the same recipe differ, we repeat the arm with all changes with another seed for the data order, the drawn views and the random rotations. The two runs differ by 0.02 dB on the held-out objects (Table 4), so differences of a few tenths of a dB between arms are larger than the variation between runs.

All three changes to how the decoder reads the scene matter. Without the footprint, the model loses 1.7 dB on the held-out objects, and 299 of the 300 objects are worse. Without the 2D embedding it loses 5.2 dB, and with 8×88\times 8 patches instead of 4×44\times 4 it loses 3.0 dB. Both cost more than before the footprint was added, 4.1 and 2.3 dB on the same harness, so with the footprint the decoder relies more on knowing where each Gaussian lands and on small patches, not less. Each change costs about as much on the training objects as on the held-out ones, so they help the model fit its training images, not only generalize. The changes matter just as much at full scale (Table 7). Trained on all objects with the recipe before the footprint, to the first milestone of the final run, the model loses 4.3 dB without the 2D embedding and 2.4 dB with 8×88\times 8 patches. The final recipe without the footprint scores 1.4 dB lower than the final model on the fresh held-out objects (Table 2), and lower on every one of the 300. Figure 9 in the appendix shows how each change looks.

Giving the decoder the footprint in its values as well as its keys, through a second zero-initialized layer per decoder layer, adds another 0.7 dB on the harness (Table 4), so the footprint can also help the decoder read the Gaussians it selects. We nevertheless keep it in the keys only. There, it only decides which Gaussians a patch attends to, which keeps a clear split between the geometry we compute and what the network learns. The values variant is also more sensitive to inputs denser than in training (Sections 6.4 and 6.5): with 40,000 Gaussians, it loses 0.3 dB more than the keys-only model (95% interval 0.2 to 0.4 dB), and for the keys-only model this loss grows with training (Section 6.4). We leave the values variant to future work.

Without the small isotropic term that we take from gsplat (0.3 square pixels), the model loses only 0.08 dB (Table 4), against 1.7 dB without the footprint, so its gain does not come from a rasterizer convention.

Restricting each patch’s cross-attention to the Gaussians that reach its tile, the way a rasterizer bins Gaussians by tile, adds only 0.2 dB and saves little time (Appendix E), so we keep dense cross-attention and let the network decide which Gaussians each patch attends to.

The first two stages change the model the most, since they turn a mesh renderer into a Gaussian one, so we test them separately, at 256 pixels on all 26,820 objects. Each arm trains for 50,000 steps, so all of them get the same number of steps: from RenderFormer’s weights with the input layer trained alone for the first 5,000 steps (our recipe), from RenderFormer’s weights with the whole model trained from the start, and from random weights. We evaluate each at 256 pixels on the held-out objects, against the unpruned render downsampled as in training (Table 10 in Appendix C.4). Training the input layer alone first gives 3.1 dB more than training the whole model from the start, in the same number of steps. The gain is not the input layer’s higher learning rate: training the whole model from the start with the input layer at the first stage’s learning rate (10−310^{-3}) does worse still, 0.55 dB below the whole model at one learning rate. Its validation loss stays flat for the first 24,000 steps before it starts to learn. We did not find a recipe that trains the model from random weights: with the loss of stages 1 and 2, it collapsed to a constant black image.

6.3 Data and training length

To see how much the amount of data matters, we fine-tune the end of stage 2 with the recipe of the harness (Section 6.2), before the footprint was added, on 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 objects and on all 26,820, with the same number of steps (Figure 4). Stage 2 has already seen all 26,820 objects, so every point is a fine-tune of a model that renders thousands of objects, and the passes over each training image differ by four orders of magnitude: about 9,400 at one object and 0.35 at 26,820. On a single object, the model fits its own training images 7 dB above rasterizing its input and forgets the other objects. With more objects the two curves approach each other and meet at the full set, about 12 dB below rasterizing the input. At our compute, the model is not data-limited. The final model, trained about 10 times longer on all objects and with the footprint, still scores about the same on its training and held-out objects (the triangles).

The final run was still improving when it ended. It gained about 0.9 dB with each doubling of its steps, from 94,000 to 375,000, with no slowdown (Table 11), so longer training would narrow the gap, by an amount these points cannot tell.

Appendix F shows how much detail the network can output when it is trained on a single object.

6.4 Where the gap comes from

Denser inputs than in training do not help the model. With 40,000 Gaussians instead of 20,000, rasterization gains 4.6 dB while the model loses 3.1 dB (Table 8), and on the real captures, more Gaussians likewise help the rasterizer and hurt the model (Table 6). It never saw inputs of that size in training. The same recipe without the footprint also loses 1.6 dB at 40,000 Gaussians, so dense cross-attention, which spreads each patch’s attention over twice as many Gaussians, is part of the cause, and the footprint, whose values shift as denser splats use smaller Gaussians, adds to it. An earlier model with windowed cross-attention, in which each patch sees only the Gaussians that reach it, lost nothing at 40,000 Gaussians, but gained nothing either. With less input, the model degrades more slowly than rasterization (Table 8), most likely because it was not reproducing that detail in the first place.

The errors are largest in fine detail. The 10% of pixels with the strongest edges in the reference hold 71% of the model’s squared error. Yet the model trails the rasterizer by more off the edges than on them, 8.1 against 6.2 dB, so part of its error lies at low frequencies, at the scale of the object’s parts (Appendix C.8). At high frequencies it both blurs and adds detail that is not in the reference: above 1/4 cycles per pixel it reproduces 85% of the reference’s content, against 93% for the rasterizer (Appendix C.9). The gap also grows with the number of Gaussians the model has to blend at a pixel, and is largest where 32 or more reach it, as on most of the object (Appendix C.10).

A reachable target does not close the gap, at least late in training. The model is trained to produce renders of the full splat, which hold detail its pruned input does not. We therefore trained the harness to reproduce the rasterization of its own input instead, a target that holds nothing the input lacks. Measured against that target, it scores only 0.19 dB more than the harness trained on the full splat (Appendix C.1). Both are short fine-tunes of a model that was trained on the full splat, though, so this shows what a reachable target changes late in training, not from the start.

Together, these results are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: the model barely uses more detail when its input has it, its fine detail is blurred and partly spurious, and a reachable target does not help. The ablations agree: all three changes that improve the model make the decoder more precise in the image (Section 6.2), and the footprint gives the most direct evidence. Each Gaussian’s footprint follows from its center, scale and rotation and the camera, all of which the decoder receives, yet giving it explicitly adds 1.4 dB at full scale, on the held-out and the training objects alike (Table 7). The decoder did not recover the footprint on its own in our training. It also reduces both kinds of error above at high frequencies: the model reproduces more of the reference’s content and adds less that the reference does not have (Appendix C.1).

Under-training is not ruled out, however. The final run was still improving, each training image was seen about four times, the larger inputs were never seen in training, and the controls above are short fine-tunes of a model trained on the full-splat target. The evidence that more encoder layers and a wider network do not help comes from an earlier model on 100 objects (Appendix E).

To test the encoder directly, we fine-tune the final model on the 14 views of one held-out object, once with only the view decoder trained and the scene encoder frozen, and once with the whole model, for 10,000 steps each. The two fit the object about equally well, both several dB above rasterizing its input (Appendix C.1). On one object, the frozen scene tokens hold what the decoder needs to exceed the rasterizer.

Appendix C.11 shows the four held-out objects where the model does worst. On all four the shapes are right, and the error comes from dense texture and soft, low-contrast structure.

6.5 Beyond the training setup

One camera configuration. The model was trained in a single camera configuration: 512×512512\times 512 pixels, a 45∘45^{\circ} field of view, and cameras at distances from 1.15 to 2.45. Table 8 in Appendix C.2 changes one factor at a time, on 30 held-out objects, and shows that the model is a renderer for that configuration, not a general one. At 256 and 1,024 pixels it drops to about 33 dB. Rasterization also loses about 4 dB at these resolutions, but the model loses about 6. For cameras much farther away than in training it breaks, at 24.09 dB. Changing the field of view costs only 1.1 dB at 35∘35^{\circ} and 1.2 dB at 60∘60^{\circ}, even when the object fills the frame as in training, while rasterization is unaffected. Without the footprint, the same model lost 2.4 and 3.2 dB at these fields of view, so telling the decoder how large each Gaussian appears also makes it far less tied to the training field of view. Cameras closer than in training cost 1.6 dB. Inputs denser than in training do not work as well: with 40,000 Gaussians the model loses 3.1 dB, against 1.6 dB without the footprint. Varying the resolution, field of view and distance during training would most likely fix the rest. Training on three camera distances instead of one mainly improved close cameras (Appendix D), and we expect the same for the other factors. Covering more configurations takes more training.

Camera paths. Rendered along a smooth 96-frame orbit that avoids every training camera, the model keeps its quality, 38.52 dB per frame on average over 30 held-out objects. It renders every frame on its own and was never trained on sequences, yet the videos show no flicker (project page, Appendix A).

Real captures. We also apply the model to regions of four real scenes from the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset (Barron et al., 2022), cut out of splats we train with gsplat and normalized like our objects, with inputs of up to 160,000 Gaussians (Appendix B). The model gets shapes, colors and layout right and softens fine texture, as on the objects. With 20,000 Gaussians, its training input size, it stays 1.6 to 4.7 dB below rasterizing the same input on the evaluation crop. With more Gaussians the rasterizer improves and the model gets worse (Section 6.4). The regions are viewed from outside on an orbit, so this is not yet rendering of full scenes.

7 Limitations

Quality and speed. GaussianRenderFormer is not yet a practical replacement for a rasterizer. It stays several dB below rasterizing the same input (Table 2), is several hundred times slower and needs far more memory (Table 3), and its time and memory grow quickly with the input (Appendix C.3).

Objects, not scenes. We train and evaluate on single objects viewed from outside, and our real captures are regions of scenes viewed the same way, so rendering a full scene, with the camera inside it, remains open. The full self-attention of the scene encoder also limits how many Gaussians the model can take (Appendix C.3).

One camera configuration. GaussianRenderFormer renders well only in its training configuration. Other input sizes, camera distances, resolutions and fields of view cost it quality, but not the rasterizer (Section 6.5).

Appearance. We use only the view-independent color of each Gaussian, so GaussianRenderFormer cannot render the view-dependent effects that 3DGS stores as spherical harmonics. Unlike RenderFormer, it also renders the colors stored in the Gaussians under fixed lighting and cannot relight them.

Input preparation. The renderer itself has no rasterizer, but preparing an input from a larger splat does use one. Pruning to 20,000 Gaussians scores each Gaussian by rasterizing it from 64 views, and the following fine-tune is ordinary 3DGS optimization (Section 5). Inputs of up to 20,000 Gaussians need neither step.

Bound to RenderFormer’s design. Starting from RenderFormer’s weights limits how far the network can change. Changes to its pretrained parts undo what the weights encode: in early experiments, even doubling the frequency of the existing position embedding hurt as much as replacing it. Only additive changes, new parts initialized to zero such as our 2D embedding, kept the pretrained behavior. More capacity on top of the pretrained layers trained without trouble but gave nothing: in an earlier version of the model, on 100 objects, 9 extra layers (287M parameters in total) and an 8 times wider feed-forward network performed exactly like the original. We could therefore add to RenderFormer’s design but not freely redesign it, and we cannot tell how a network designed for Gaussians from the start would do.

Cost and dependence on RenderFormer. Training the model is expensive (Appendix G), and we found no recipe that trains it from random weights (Section 6.2), so it depends on a pretrained mesh renderer.

8 Conclusion

We presented GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that renders a given set of 3D Gaussians into an image with no rasterizer in the renderer. Starting from RenderFormer’s weights, a token per Gaussian, a 2D rotary embedding of where each Gaussian lands in the image, its projected footprint and smaller patches are enough for a network to render objects it has never seen, in the camera configuration it was trained in. A clear gap to rasterizing the same input remains. It is not a generalization gap, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder, though under-training is not ruled out. A learned renderer for Gaussians is feasible, but not yet competitive with a rasterizer.

Each limitation in Section 7 points to future work. Giving each Gaussian material parameters, as relightable Gaussian methods do, and adding light sources to the scene would let a model like ours learn relighting and global illumination, the goal that motivates this work (Section 1).

Appendix A Camera paths

We render 30 held-out objects along a smooth path of 96 frames that makes one full turn around the object. The camera distance varies smoothly between 1.35 and 2.05, inside the training range, and the elevation rises and falls twice per turn. The angles are offset so that no frame repeats a training camera. Every frame is rendered by the model from the 20,000-Gaussian input, by gsplat from the same input, and by gsplat from the full splat (the reference).

We report the PSNR of each frame against the reference, on the evaluation crop as in the main evaluation, and a simple measure of consistency between frames. For each pair of consecutive frames we take the change from one frame to the next, for the model and for the reference, and compute the PSNR between the two changes over the whole frame. A model that flickers adds changes the reference does not have and scores lower. This measure does not separate flicker from ordinary per-frame error, so we compare it with gsplat on the input and also inspect the videos. Table 5 shows the results and Figure 5 shows frames of one path.

The model’s per-frame quality along the path matches its quality on the evaluation views (38.36 dB on the 4 views of the held-out objects), so it does not depend on the training cameras. Its consistency score is 4.8 dB below gsplat’s, a little less than its per-frame gap of 5.6 dB, and the videos on the project page show no visible flicker.

Appendix B Real captures

We use four scenes of the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset: bonsai, counter, garden and kitchen. The dataset’s project page states no license, but the project page of SMERF, by an overlapping group of authors, states that the Mip-NeRF 360 scenes are released under CC BY 4.0.44 4 https://smerf-3d.github.io/#data No trained splat of them carries a clear license, so we train our own. We use gsplat with its standard recipe and densification, 30,000 steps on the images downsampled 4 times, with only the view-independent color, and hold out every 8th image. We then cut out a cube around the point the cameras look at, drop Gaussians larger than a quarter of the cube, and normalize the region like our training objects. The reference is a rasterization of every Gaussian in the region, the input is the region pruned with our pipeline (Section 5), and we render 7 orbit views above the horizon at distance 1.7. Table 6 lists the results. The PSNR here is over the whole frame, which is mostly background, so it is not comparable to the object-level numbers in the main text.

The model does best at its training input size of 20,000 Gaussians, where it stays 1.6 to 4.7 dB below rasterizing the same input on the evaluation crop (29.8 against 31.4 dB on bonsai, 29.7 against 32.3 on counter, 28.9 against 30.9 on garden and 30.6 against 35.4 on kitchen, means over the 7 views). With 80,000 and 160,000 Gaussians the rasterizer improves by up to 13 dB, while the model gets worse (Section 6.4). Figure 7 shows the best and the worst view of each scene, by the model’s PSNR on the crop, with 20,000 Gaussians. In all four scenes the model gets the shapes, colors and layout right and softens fine texture, most visibly on the bonsai’s foliage and on the objects on the counter. Gaussians cut in half by the region’s boundary, and long thin Gaussians at the edge of what the photos covered, show up as blurry streaks in both the reference and the model, which smears them further.

Figure 6 shows the bonsai region at the three input sizes.

Appendix C Additional results

C.1 Supporting measurements

Harness schedule.

Every harness arm starts from the end of stage 2 and trains for 3,000 steps at 256 pixels with log-L1 only (warmup of 101 steps, cosine decay over the last 1,000), then for 33,000 steps at 512 pixels with log-L1 and LPIPS (warmup of 1,000 steps, decay over the last 3,000), at a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} with a batch of 8 views on 8 GPUs.

Full scale.

Table 7 repeats the ablations of Section 6.2 at full scale. The arms before the footprint are trained on all 26,820 objects for 94,000 steps plus a 10,000-step decay, the first milestone of the final run, and evaluated on the 4 views of the development held-out objects. The footprint pair is the final model and the same recipe trained without the footprint, on all 28 views. With the footprint, the model reproduces more of the reference’s content above 1/4 cycles per pixel, 85% against 83% without it (measured as in Appendix C.9), and the content it adds that is not in the reference falls by 24 to 38% between 1/16 and 1/4 cycles per pixel.

Reachable target.

Measured against the rasterization of its own input, the harness trained on that target scores 33.24 dB on the held-out objects and 35.04 dB on its own training images, against 33.05 and 34.80 dB for the harness trained on the full splat: 0.19 dB more (95% interval over objects 0.17 to 0.21 dB, one run per arm).

Frozen encoder.

Fine-tuned on the 14 views of object 604 for 10,000 steps, the final model reaches 45.7 dB on these views with only the view decoder trained and 46.4 dB with the whole model (47.2 and 46.8 dB a thousand steps earlier), against 41.8 dB for rasterizing its input and 34.5 dB before the fine-tune.

Table 8 changes one factor at a time from the training setup (Section 6.5).

Table 9 gives the time and memory of one view as the input grows from 20,000 to 640,000 Gaussians.

Table 10 compares the initializations and schedules of the first two stages (Section 6.2).

C.5 Training curve

Figure 8 shows the validation loss of the final run at 512 pixels. Table 11 shows the held-out PSNR at four points of the run, each after a 10,000-step learning-rate decay. The run was still improving when it ended, by less in each quarter. Section 6.3 discusses what that means for the gap.

C.6 Renders of the ablations

Figure 9 shows the harness arms and the full-scale models of Section 6.2 on objects of Figure 3.

C.7 Spread over objects

Figure 10 shows how the PSNR is spread over the 300 fresh held-out objects, over all 28 views. The model ranges from 26.5 to 45.0 dB, with a median of 38.2 dB, and gsplat on the input ranges from 36.4 to 49.3 dB.

C.8 Error on edges

We rank the pixels of each held-out crop by the Sobel gradient of the gray reference. On the 10% of pixels with the strongest edges, the model scores 30.04 dB, against 45.19 dB on the rest, and these pixels hold 71% of its squared error. Rasterizing the input shows the same pattern, with 78% of its error on these pixels. The model trails the rasterizer by 6.2 dB on the edges and by 8.1 dB on the rest of the object. In the frequency domain, 72% of the model’s error energy lies above 1/8 cycles per pixel, but its error also exceeds the rasterizer’s at low frequencies (Table 12).

C.9 Error by frequency band

Table 12 splits the error of each held-out view into frequency bands. We take the square crop around the object at its native resolution, apply a Hann window, and sum the squared magnitude of the 2D Fourier transform over octave bands of radial frequency. For each band we report the share of each renderer’s error energy, its in-phase gain, the part of the reference’s content that it reproduces (g=Re​∑Fx​Fr∗/∑|Fr|2g=\mathrm{Re}\sum F_{x}F_{r}^{*}/\sum|F_{r}|^{2}, 1 when all of it is kept), its unmatched power, the content that is not in the reference (∑|Fx−g​Fr|2/∑|Fr|2\sum|F_{x}-gF_{r}|^{2}/\sum|F_{r}|^{2}, 0 when there is none), and the model’s error energy divided by the rasterizer’s. Means over the 1,200 views of the 300 held-out objects.

At the highest frequencies the model reproduces 85% of the reference’s content, against 93% for the rasterizer, and adds almost four times as much content that is not in the reference: it both blurs and adds spurious detail. This is not a small misalignment: if every 16×1616\times 16 tile of an image may shift by up to 2 pixels to best match the reference, the model’s error drops by only 4%, and the rasterizer’s by 0.7%. Its excess error over the rasterizer is largest, relative to the rasterizer’s, at the lowest frequencies. This is not a global error in brightness or contrast: fitting a gain and a bias per view and color channel to the reference raises the model’s PSNR by only 0.05 dB. It is error at the scale of the object’s parts.

C.10 Error by overlap

A typical pixel of an object is reached by about 130 of its 20,000 Gaussians, and 77% of the object’s pixels are reached by 32 or more. Table 13 groups the pixels of each held-out view by the number of input Gaussians that reach them, counted as the Gaussians whose opacity at that pixel is at least 1/2551/255, the ones a rasterizer blends there, without stopping at opaque ones. Both renderers score best on pixels reached by a single Gaussian, and lowest on pixels reached by 16 to 63, which lie mostly on the silhouette and on thin parts. The gap between the two is smallest where one to three Gaussians reach a pixel.

Appendix D The road to the final model

Several choices in Section 4 only make sense in light of what did not work, so we summarize the experiments that led to them. Early results used other protocols, so we report most of them only qualitatively.

D.1 Data

Our first training set followed RenderFormer’s examples, meshes sampled into Gaussians with RenderFormer’s own renders as the target. The model learned to imitate RenderFormer’s lighting instead of rendering its input, so we switched to real splats rendered by gsplat. Scenes composed of several small splats then plateaued whatever we changed, and tests on outside captures showed that the quality of the input mattered more than its size. We moved to single Objaverse_Splats objects, from 2,667 to 13,405 and finally 26,820, and added the fine-tune of the pruned input (Section 5).

D.2 Training schedule

Training the input layer alone first was part of our design from the start, since RenderFormer’s pretrained layers expect its own triangle tokens. A series of runs that skipped this stage because of a bug all stalled at the same loss, whatever encoding of the Gaussian parameters they used, and restoring the stage fixed them. The stage ablation of Section 6.2 tests this directly. Larger inputs (20,000 Gaussians instead of 5,000), random rotations of every sample and much longer training with a 256 to 512 pixel curriculum each helped clearly. The best model of this phase, trained on 13,405 objects, scored 30.39 dB on our held-out set.

D.3 The decoder

That model scored only 0.55 dB better on its training objects than on held-out ones, models trained on 10 to 1,000 objects could not fit even their own training objects, and more layers or a wider network did not help (Appendix E). We therefore tested changes to the view decoder on 10 training objects. The 2D rotary embedding of projected positions was the first change that improved both training and held-out objects. Smaller patches improved them further, and became affordable once the view decoder ran in bf16 with gradient checkpointing, which made a training step about three times faster. We also tried windowed cross-attention at this point and later dropped it (Section 6.2). Showing every object from three distances mainly improved close cameras. The final model combines these changes and trains on all 26,820 objects for 375,000 steps, from the second-stage checkpoint of the previous phase (Appendix G).

Appendix E Changes that did not help

Table 14 lists changes we tried that did not improve the model. Most were tested on small training sets with earlier versions of the model, so they do not rule a change out at full scale, but none of them justified a full run. Margins are the PSNR of the rasterized input minus the model’s, so lower is better.

Per-object training, which can beat the rasterizer on single objects but does not transfer, is described in Appendix F.

Appendix F Training on a single object

Our main model shares one set of weights across all objects. Here we ask what the same architecture can do when it only has to render one object, which separates what the network can represent from what it can learn to generalize. All of these experiments used earlier versions of the model.

Trained on a single object with 9,000 views of its full splat, an earlier version of the model ended above rasterizing the pruned input on 4 of the 13 objects we tried, by up to 1.8 dB. It does so by learning the object and filling in what pruning removed, not by rendering its input better: the one such model we kept scores 44.59 dB against the full splat but only 42.18 dB against a rasterization of its own input. These runs show how much detail the network can output for one object, not what sharing the weights costs.

F.1 How much detail can the network output

We first trained the model on a single object, a scan of tomatoes, on its 14 training views and without augmentation, until it had memorized them. On those views it reached 52.5 to 53.0 dB on average against the full splat, with an LPIPS of 0.0003, and its renders cannot be told apart from the reference (Figure 12). The decoder can therefore output this much detail when it is trained to, so the error of our general model is not a hard limit of its output head. This experiment used an earlier input: the 219,000-Gaussian scan pruned to 20,000 with the same importance score, but without the fine-tune of Section 5, so rasterizing it gives a blurry image. On new views between the training views, the model’s renders are much sharper than that rasterization. They are closer to the full splat in PSNR (30.5 against 29.7 dB) and far closer in LPIPS (0.09 against 0.15 on the crops of Figure 12), and far from the rasterization of the model’s own input (27.4 dB). From 14 views of the full splat, the model learned enough of the object to restore much of what pruning removed. It did not learn all of it: on new views it stays far below its 52.5 dB on the training views.

F.2 Compensating for pruning on one object

With thousands of views of the object instead of 14, per-object training can beat the rasterizer on new views. The training images are renders of the full splat, so the model learns that one object and can fill in what pruning removed from its input. This is a prior on the object, not a better rendering of the input. We trained on 9,000 random views per object, in cycles of 30,000 steps with a cosine learning rate, and evaluated on 40 views not used in training (24 random, 8 close-up and 8 distant), against gsplat on the same 20,000-Gaussian input. Table 15 and Figure 13 show the results. Only on 4 of the 13 objects we tried did the model end above the rasterizer on average, by up to 1.8 dB, and most of its gain was in close-up views, where the pruned input shows its gaps. On the other 9 it stayed below, by 1 to 9 dB, typically on simple objects that the 20,000 Gaussians already render almost perfectly.

Of these models, we kept only the one trained on the tomatoes. On the same 40 views, it scores 44.59 dB against the full splat and 42.18 dB against a rasterization of its own input, while that rasterization scores 43.29 dB against the full splat. The model is further from its own input than from the full splat on all 40 views, and most of all close up (37.90 against 41.90 dB). It has learned to reproduce the object, not to render its input more faithfully.

F.3 Why we do not pursue it

These results show that the network can output far more detail than our general model does, and that trained on one object it can learn to fill in what pruning removed. We do not consider per-object training a practical use of it, for three reasons. It does not transfer to shared weights (Section 6.3). It is expensive to store and to run: every object needs its own copy of the 195M-parameter network, about 745 MB, to improve on an input of 20,000 Gaussians that takes 1.1 MB, and rendering a view took 476 ms against 1 ms for gsplat in our measurement on an NVIDIA A40. It is also slow to train, with 4 to 5 cycles of 30,000 steps per object. We tried to cut the storage with low-rank adapters (LoRA) on a shared network, but they fell short of the rasterizer at equal storage. The gain, under 2 dB on the objects where it works, does not justify this cost.

Appendix G Reproducibility

The code, the trained weights, the checkpoint after the first two stages, the lists of training and evaluation objects, and the scripts for every experiment in this paper are available at https://github.com/SVLwoof/gaussianformer. Its file paper/README.md gives the command and the expected numbers for every table and figure. The three trained models are on Hugging Face: the final model (shahafvl/gaussianformer-v22), the model without the footprint (shahafvl/gaussianformer-v21) and the checkpoint after stage 2 (shahafvl/gaussianformer-256px). Table 1 describes the released training recipe. The final model was produced by that recipe, with two differences in its first two stages, which were run during earlier phases of the project. Its first stage was trained on 13,405 objects instead of 26,820, and its first two stages saw only the 14 views at distance 1.7, not all 28. Starting from the released checkpoint after the second stage reproduces stages 3 and 4 exactly, which is about 620 of the 1,327 GPU-hours. Running all four stages from RenderFormer’s weights with the released recipe is documented, but we have not run it end to end.

The stages of the final model took 46 GPU-hours (stage 1) and 662 GPU-hours (stage 2) on NVIDIA L40S GPUs, 592 GPU-hours for stages 3 and 4 up to 375,000 steps (91 on A40 and 501 on RTX Pro 6000 GPUs, as the cluster allowed) and 27 GPU-hours for the final decay on L40S GPUs.

Table 16 lists the settings of the final model. All of them are options of the released code.

Licenses

Objaverse_Splats states no license of its own. Its splats are fit to Objaverse objects, a collection released under ODC-By 1.0 in which each object keeps its creator’s Creative Commons license. We release our code and trained weights under the MIT license, as RenderFormer does.
